lessons.title: Ways to Own Gold and Silver in India: Physical, ETFs, SGBs, EGRs and MCX

children.text: Ask ten Indian families how they own gold and nine will say jewellery. Ask a younger investor and you may hear gold ETFs, Sovereign Gold Bonds, a "digital gold" button in a payments app, or MCX Gold Petal. These routes all track the same metal, but they differ enormously in cost, safety, liquidity, regulation and tax. Choose badly and you can lose 10% or more to charges before gold even moves. By the end of this lesson you will know every major route to own gold and silver in India, what each one really costs, who regulates it, and how to match the route to your purpose.

body.text: Pick the route by purpose. Jewellery is for wearing, not investing. ETFs, gold funds and Sovereign Gold Bonds are for holding. MCX futures are for hedging and trading. Mixing up these purposes is where most of the money gets lost.

children.text: Route 1: Physical Gold and Silver
Jewellery, coins and bars are the most familiar route, and the most expensive one for investment purposes.
Making charges.
Jewellers add making charges, often somewhere between 8% and 25% of the gold value depending on design, and these are usually lost when you sell.
GST.
3% GST applies on the purchase.
Resale deductions.
Jewellers typically buy back at the gold value, sometimes minus a deduction for purity testing or melting losses. Many banks sell gold coins but do not buy them back.
Storage and safety.
Bank lockers cost money every year, and home storage carries theft risk.

body.label: Hallmarking
body.context: Gold jewellery sold by jewellers must carry a BIS hallmark with a unique 6-digit Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID). You can verify it using the BIS Care app before you buy.

body.title: The real cost of a necklace
body.prompt: Anjali buys a 20 gram, 22 karat necklace in Pune. The 22 karat rate is ₹9,200 per gram, making charges are 12% of the gold value, and GST is 3% on the gold value plus making charges. What is the total she pays, to the nearest rupee?
body.explanation: Gold value = 20 × ₹9,200 = ₹1,84,000. Making charges = 12% × ₹1,84,000 = ₹22,080. Subtotal = ₹2,06,080. GST = 3% × ₹2,06,080 = ₹6,182. Total = ₹2,12,262. If she sold it the next day at the same gold rate and received only the gold value of ₹1,84,000, she would lose ₹28,262, about 13% of what she paid.

body.title: Before buying physical gold or silver
steps: Check the HUID hallmark on gold jewellery and verify it on the BIS Care app.
Confirm the purity (22 karat, 24 karat, 999 silver) and the exact weight on the invoice.
Ask for making charges as a separate line item, not buried in the rate.
Ask about the buyback or exchange policy, including any deductions, before paying.

children.text: Route 2: Gold and Silver ETFs

markDefs.definition: An exchange-traded fund, regulated by SEBI, that holds physical gold of standard purity and trades on NSE and BSE like a share. Each unit represents a small quantity of gold.

children.text: A
gold ETF

is a SEBI-regulated mutual fund scheme that holds physical gold and trades on NSE and BSE like a share. India's first, now known as Nippon India ETF Gold BeES, launched in 2007. Silver ETFs followed after SEBI permitted them, with the first launching in 2022.
No purity or storage worries.
The fund holds standard-purity metal with a custodian.
Low cost.
You pay brokerage and an annual expense ratio built into the price, with no making charges.
Liquid.
Buy and sell any time during market hours through your demat account on Zerodha, Groww or any broker.
Small tracking differences.
The ETF price can differ slightly from the gold price because of expenses, cash holdings and market demand.

markDefs.definition: Fund of funds schemes that invest in gold ETFs. They allow SIPs without a demat account, at a slightly higher total cost than holding the ETF directly.

children.text: If you do not have a demat account,
gold mutual funds
invest in gold ETFs for you, and allow SIPs, at a slightly higher overall cost.
Route 3: Sovereign Gold Bonds

markDefs.definition: Government of India securities issued by the RBI and denominated in grams of gold. They pay 2.5% annual interest on the issue price and redeem at the prevailing gold price.

children.text: Sovereign Gold Bonds
(SGBs) are government securities issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, denominated in grams of gold. For long-term holders, they were the most rewarding route of all.
Gold price plus interest.
You get the rupee price of gold at redemption, plus 2.5% a year interest on the issue price, paid half-yearly.
Eight-year tenure.
Early redemption is allowed from the fifth year on interest payment dates.
Tax-free at maturity.
For individuals, capital gains on redemption at maturity are exempt. Interest is taxable at your slab rate.
Sovereign credit.
No default risk beyond that of the Government of India, and no storage or purity concerns.

stats.label: Interest
stats.context: On the original issue price, every year for 8 years

body.title: What 10 grams of the first SGB earned
body.prompt: An investor bought 10 grams of the first SGB at ₹2,684 per gram and held it to maturity at ₹6,132 per gram, receiving 2.5% interest a year on the issue price for 8 years. Before tax on interest, what was the total gain (capital gain plus interest) in rupees?
body.explanation: Investment = ₹26,840. Capital gain = (₹6,132 minus ₹2,684) × 10 = ₹34,480, tax-free at maturity. Interest = 2.5% × ₹26,840 × 8 years = ₹5,368. Total gain = ₹39,848, about 148% on the original investment.

body.text: The government has not issued new SGB tranches since February 2024. You can still buy existing SGBs in the secondary market on NSE and BSE, but trading volumes are often thin, and prices can sit at a premium or discount to the gold value. Check the price against the current gold rate, the interest dates and the remaining tenure before you buy.

children.text: Route 4: Digital Gold
Payments and investment apps let you buy "digital gold" for as little as ₹1, backed by gold that a private provider says it stores for you in a vault.

body.text: Digital gold is not regulated by SEBI or the RBI. SEBI has barred registered stock brokers from offering it, and has cautioned investors that such products fall outside its regulatory framework. You rely on the provider's own vaulting and trustee arrangements, pay 3% GST on purchase, and usually face a buy-sell spread. If you want small, regular gold purchases, a gold ETF or gold mutual fund SIP offers regulated alternatives.

body.title: Who is watching?
body.question: Which of these routes to owning gold falls outside the regulatory oversight of SEBI and the RBI?
options: Digital gold bought through a payments app
body.explanation: Gold ETFs and MCX futures are regulated by SEBI, and SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the government. Digital gold sold through apps is not covered by either regulator, so your protection depends on the provider.

children.text: Route 5: Electronic Gold Receipts

body.title: What EGRs are, and why few investors use them yet

markDefs.definition: Exchange-traded securities representing gold held in vaults of SEBI-accredited vault managers. They can be traded on stock exchanges and converted into physical gold.

children.text: Electronic Gold Receipts

(EGRs) were created under a SEBI framework to build a transparent, exchange-based spot market for gold. They represent physical gold deposited in vaults run by SEBI-accredited vault managers, and BSE and NSE have launched EGR segments.
Each EGR is backed by specific physical gold of defined purity.
EGRs can be traded on the exchange and converted back into physical gold.
They aim to give jewellers, bullion dealers and investors a transparent, national gold price.
The idea is sound, but trading volumes remain very low. For most individual investors today, gold ETFs are far more liquid for the same basic exposure.
Route 6: MCX Futures and Options
You already know how these work from Chapter 2. As a way to own gold or silver, they have a distinct profile.
Leverage.
You control far more metal than your margin, which magnifies both gains and losses.
Small contracts are available.
Gold Petal (1 gram) and Gold Guinea (8 grams) allow very small positions, and Silver Micro covers 1 kg.
Built for trading and hedging.
Contracts expire, so long-term holding means repeated rollovers, roll costs, and delivery rules near expiry.
Tax treatment differs.
Profits from commodity derivatives are taxed as business income, not capital gains. Chapter 6 covers this.
Putting It All Together

body.caption: Routes to own gold and silver in India compared

cells: Sell to jeweller, at a discount
Fund expense plus underlying ETF expense
RBI, for the Government of India
Long-term holding, if bought at a fair price

body.title: How the main investment routes are taxed (high level)

children.text: Tax rules for gold changed significantly with the Union Budget of July 2024 and later amendments, and can change again. As a broad guide under the rules applicable for financial year 2025-26:
Physical gold and silver: long-term if held more than 24 months, taxed at 12.5% without indexation; otherwise at your slab rate.
Gold and silver ETFs: long-term if held more than 12 months, taxed at 12.5%; otherwise at your slab rate.
Gold mutual funds (fund of funds): long-term if held more than 24 months, taxed at 12.5%; otherwise at your slab rate.
SGBs: interest taxed at slab rate; gains on redemption at maturity exempt for individuals; gains on sale in the secondary market taxed as capital gains.
MCX futures and options: treated as business income, covered in Chapter 6.
Confirm the current rules with a chartered accountant before acting, especially for large amounts.

columns.label: If you want to hold gold for years
points: Gold ETFs or gold mutual funds for regulated, low-cost exposure
Existing SGBs in the secondary market, if priced fairly
No leverage, no expiry, no margin calls
Accept that gold can go flat for years

columns.label: If you want to trade or hedge gold
points: MCX futures or options, sized carefully
Positions must be rolled or closed before expiry and delivery periods
Requires active monitoring and risk limits

body.title: Check the hallmark
body.textWithBlank: Hallmarked gold jewellery in India carries a ___-digit HUID that buyers can verify on the BIS Care app.
body.explanation: The 6-digit Hallmark Unique Identification links each piece of jewellery to its hallmarking record, so you can confirm purity claims before paying.

body.title: Planning for a wedding in eight years
body.scenario: Kavita, a 41-year-old school principal in Lucknow, wants to set aside about ₹5,00,000 in gold over the coming years for her daughter's wedding, around eight years away. Her options, according to relatives: buy jewellery now "before prices rise", buy digital gold on her payments app every month, or open an MCX account because "futures give more gold for less money".
body.prompt: Evaluate each suggestion, and describe a more sensible way to think about the routes for her goal.
body.modelAnswer:
Jewellery now: she would pay making charges and GST today, lose a large share of those if designs change and she exchanges pieces later, and carry storage risk for eight years. Designs chosen eight years early may not suit the wedding.

Monthly digital gold: convenient, but outside SEBI and RBI regulation, with 3% GST on each purchase and a buy-sell spread. Over eight years, those costs and the provider risk add up.

MCX futures: leverage is the opposite of what a long-term goal needs. Contracts expire, need rollovers and margin, and losses can exceed the margin posted. This route is for trading and hedging.

A more sensible way to think: separate the investment goal from the jewellery purchase. For the eight-year accumulation, regulated low-cost routes such as a gold ETF, a gold mutual fund SIP, or existing SGBs bought at a fair secondary market price fit the purpose. Closer to the wedding, she can sell and buy the jewellery she actually wants, paying making charges once, on designs chosen at that time. The right allocation for her overall situation is a question for a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

body.title: Ways to Own Gold and Silver

cards.definition: The 6-digit Hallmark Unique Identification on BIS-hallmarked gold jewellery.
The jeweller's charge for crafting, often 8% to 25% of gold value, usually lost on resale.
SEBI-regulated fund holding physical gold, traded on NSE and BSE through a demat account.
A fund of funds that invests in gold ETFs and allows SIPs without a demat account.
RBI-issued government security in grams of gold, paying 2.5% interest, with tax-free gains at maturity for individuals.
App-based gold backed by a private provider's vault, outside SEBI and RBI regulation.
An exchange-traded security backed by gold in a SEBI-accredited vault, convertible to physical gold.

points: Jewellery is for wearing: making charges, GST and resale deductions can cost 10% or more on day one.
Gold and silver ETFs, and gold mutual funds for SIPs, are regulated, low-cost routes for long-term holding.
SGBs combined gold returns with 2.5% interest and tax-free maturity gains; no new tranches since February 2024, but existing bonds trade on exchanges.
Digital gold is outside SEBI and RBI regulation, so treat it with caution.
EGRs offer an exchange-based spot gold market, but liquidity is still very low.
MCX futures and options are for hedging and trading, with leverage, expiries and business income tax treatment.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. Prices used in exercises are illustrative except where stated as historical. Tax rules, SGB availability and product regulations change; confirm current rules with a chartered accountant and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
